statement: A data set of $12$ numbers has a mean of $50$ and a standard deviation of $8$. A $13$th number, $50$, is added to the data set. Which of the following best describes how the mean and the standard deviation change?

choices.text: The mean stays the same, and the standard deviation increases.
choices.misconception: I thought that adding more values always spreads a data set out more, so the standard deviation had to go up.

choices.text: The mean stays the same, and the standard deviation stays the same.
choices.misconception: I thought a value sitting exactly at the mean has no effect at all, but it adds a distance of 0 while increasing the number of values.

choices.text: The mean increases, and the standard deviation stays the same.
choices.misconception: I thought adding any positive number makes the mean go up, but a new value equal to the mean leaves the mean unchanged.

choices.text: The mean stays the same, and the standard deviation decreases.

hints: How far is the new value from the mean?
Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. Think about what happens to the average distance when you add a value whose distance is $0$.
The new value adds $0$ to the sum of squared distances but raises the count from $12$ to $13$, so the average squared distance shrinks.

solutions.reliable: The new mean is $\frac{12 \times 50 + 50}{13} = \frac{650}{13} = 50$, so the mean is unchanged. The standard deviation is built from the squared distances of the values from the mean. The new value is $0$ from the mean, so the sum of squared distances stays the same while the number of values goes up from $12$ to $13$. Dividing the same total by a larger number gives a smaller result, so the standard deviation decreases.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
